AccountResponse.description: An account, as the API describes it. Never carries a hash.

is_admin.description:
Whether the account holds the seeded administrator role.

Kept because clients read it. It is now derived rather than stored, and
it answers a narrower question than `permissions` does — somebody in a
role that grants `users:read` and nothing else is not an administrator
but can still reach one administrative endpoint. New clients should read
`permissions`.

must_change_password.description:
Whether the account must set a new password before doing anything else.

Set on the administrator generated at first run. A client seeing this
should send the user to a change-password screen and nowhere else.

permissions.description:
Everything this account is allowed to do.

`resource:verb` strings. The set a client should decide what to show
from — a screen that guesses from `is_admin` will be wrong for every
role between "member" and "everything".

roles.description: The roles it is in, by name.

AdminUserResponse.description:
One account, as an administrator sees it.

The same shape a person sees of themselves. There is nothing extra to show:
this service stores no profile, and the one thing an administrator can change
is already a field.

Capabilities.description:
Body of `GET /api/v1/capabilities`.

# Why this endpoint exists

`openapi.json` is a build artefact: it describes every endpoint the software
has. Which of them an *instance* exposes is a runtime decision its operator
made. A single-page app generated from the contract therefore cannot know
whether to render a login button — the contract says login exists, and on
this deployment it may not.

So the contract describes the whole surface and this reports the subset in
force. It is deliberately unauthenticated: a client needs the answer before
it can know whether logging in is even possible.

account_password_min_length.description:
Shortest *account* password this instance accepts, so a client can say so
before the round trip rather than after it.

Named for what it governs because there are two minimums and they are
deliberately different — see
[`share_password_min_length`](Self::share_password_min_length).

accounts.description:
Whether accounts exist at all on this instance.

`false` means there is no registration, no login and no session — the
shape for a personal instance behind a VPN.

admin.description:
Whether the administrative endpoints are mounted.

The administration front-end is a separate deployment, so this says only
that the API half is present.

anonymous_upload.description:
Whether a caller without a session may upload.

Independent of [`accounts`](Self::accounts): an instance can have
accounts *and* accept anonymous uploads, which is the default.

default_expiry_hours.description:
How long a share lasts when the uploader does not choose, in hours.

The upload form needs this to say what "leave it alone" means. `null`
when this instance lets shares live forever by default.

max_expiry_hours.description:
The longest lifetime an uploader may ask for, in hours.

`null` when there is no ceiling. A form that knows this can bound its own
control instead of letting somebody pick a date the server will refuse.

max_upload_bytes.description: Longest accepted request body, in bytes.

password_reset.description:
Whether this instance can send a password reset link.

`false` when no relay is configured, which is the default. A client that
draws the "forgot password" link regardless would send people to an
endpoint that answers 404 — so this is the difference between a missing
feature and a broken one.

registration.description:
Who may create an account. Meaningless when
[`accounts`](Self::accounts) is `false`.

registration_requires_confirmation.description:
Whether registering sends a confirmation link rather than creating the
account outright.

`true` means `POST /auth/register` answers `202` and nothing exists
until the address is confirmed — so a client must show "check your
inbox" rather than treating the response as a sign-in. `false` means it
answers `201` with a session, which is what an instance that sends no
mail does.

share_password_min_length.description:
Shortest password an uploader may put on a share.

Lower than the account minimum on purpose: a share password is a second
factor on a link that is already unguessable, and it gets read out over
the phone. A form that validated share passwords against the account
rule would refuse the four-digit code the server would have accepted.

storage_remaining_bytes.description:
How much of the instance's storage quota is left, in bytes.

`null` for everyone but an administrator, and also for an administrator
when the instance has no quota set.

Only an administrator, because on a public instance this is the
operator's capacity planning and not the visitor's business: telling
every anonymous uploader how close the disk is to full invites somebody
to close the gap. An uploader who exceeds it gets a `507` naming the
limit, which is the moment they actually need to know.

version.description:
Version of the running server, for a client that wants to warn about a
mismatch with the contract it was generated from.

current_password.description:
The password in force now. Required even though the caller is signed in:
it is what stops a borrowed, unlocked browser from taking the account.

expires_in_days.description: How many days it lasts, or `null` for one that never expires.

note.description: What to call it, so a list of them means something.

uses.description:
How many accounts this code may create.

One code with several places is what the feature is for: something to
send to a group rather than a code per person. `1` makes it single-use.

expires_in_days.description:
How long the token should last, in days. Omit for a token that lives
until it is revoked.

name.description: A label for the token, so its owner can recognise it later.

code.description:
**Shown once.** Only its SHA-256 digest is stored, so this value cannot
be read back afterwards — not by an administrator, not by anybody.

CreatedInviteResponse.description: A freshly minted invite, with its code.

allOf.description: The token's metadata, identical to what a listing returns.

secret.description:
The secret, in full.

**Shown once.** Only its SHA-256 digest is stored, so this value cannot be
recovered — a client that does not keep it has to issue another token.

CreatedTokenResponse.description: A newly issued token. The only response that ever carries the secret.

ErrorBody.description: The JSON body returned for every non-2xx response.

code.description: Stable identifier the client can branch on.

message.description: Human-readable explanation. Never contains internal details.

ErrorCode.description:
Stable, machine-readable identifier for an [`Error`].

Clients branch on this; the human-readable `message` is free to change.

build_rev.description:
Commit the running binary was built from, or `unknown` outside a git
checkout. Between releases this is what identifies a build.

status.description: Where the process is in its lifecycle.

uptime_seconds.description: Whole seconds since the process started.

InviteResponse.description:
One invite code, as an administrator sees it.

Never carries the code. Only its digest is stored, so there is nothing to
show — see [`CreatedInviteResponse`] for the one moment there is.

active.description:
Whether it would still admit somebody.

Sent rather than left to the client to work out from `used`, `max_uses`
and `expires_at` against its own clock — the same reason a session says
whether it is active.

expires_at.description: When it stops working, or `null` for one that does not.

max_uses.description: How many accounts it may create.

identifier.description: Username or email address; either is accepted.

password.description:
The account's password.

Bounded by what any instance could ever have accepted rather than by the
policy in force, so that raising the minimum cannot lock out an account
whose password was valid when it was chosen.
What to set the password to.

email.description: The address to send the link to.

PublicShareResponse.description:
A share as a public visitor sees it.

Everything but `code`, `kind` and `has_password` is withheld until the share
is unlocked. A file name and a size are a description of the content, and a
password-protected share should not describe itself to somebody who has not
presented the password — the same reason its link preview must not.

expires_at.description: When it stops being served, RFC 3339.

has_password.description: Whether a password must be presented before anything else is revealed.

size_bytes.description: Size of the content in bytes.

unlocked.description: Whether the fields below are filled in.

uses_remaining.description: How many retrievals remain, or `null` for unlimited.

email.description: Address to reach the account at.

invite_code.description:
An invite code, on an instance that asks for one.

Ignored where registration is open, so a client does not have to know
which kind of instance it is talking to before filling in the form.
`/capabilities` says which it is.

username.description:
3–32 characters: letters, digits, `_` and `-`, starting with a letter or
digit. Stored lowercased.

ServiceStatus.description:
Where the process is in its lifecycle.

Load balancers and `docker healthcheck` need to distinguish "still migrating"
from "draining" from "healthy"; a bare 200/500 cannot express that.

SessionResponse.description:
One sign-in, as the API describes it.

Covers sessions that are over as well as the ones that work. Somebody reading
this list is usually asking whether anybody else has been in, and a session
that was revoked last Tuesday is exactly what they need to see.

active.description:
Whether it still works.

Sent rather than left to the client to derive from `expires_at`: a
browser's clock can be wrong by more than a session's remaining life, and
being told "this is still live" by a machine with a fast clock is how
somebody decides not to revoke something they should have.

created_ip.description:
Where the sign-in came from, when there was an answer worth recording.

`null` on an instance that sits behind an undeclared proxy, and on
sessions that predate this being recorded.

created_user_agent.description:
The `User-Agent` the sign-in arrived with, exactly as it was sent.

Not parsed into "Chrome on macOS": doing that reliably is famously hard,
and getting it wrong tells somebody a session is theirs when it is not.
created_user_agent.example: Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7) Safari/605.1.15

current.description:
Whether this is the session reading the list.

The one thing a person cannot work out for themselves, and the one they
need before ending anything.

ended_reason.description:
Why it ended early, if somebody ended it.

`null` means it simply ran out. The values are `signed_out`, `revoked`,
`password_changed` and `password_reset`.

expires_at.description: When it stops, or stopped, working.

last_seen_at.description: When this session was last used.

ShareBody.description:
The request body of `POST /shares`: the content itself, as bytes.

A named type only so the contract can say `format: binary`. Declaring the
body as `Vec<u8>` makes utoipa emit an *array of integers*, which a docs UI
renders as a JSON array editor and a generated client types as `number[]` —
neither of which can carry a file.

An empty body is refused with a `400`, and that rule is *not* expressible
here: `min_length` is a field-level attribute, and the field's own schema is
overridden by the `value_type` above — which has to stay, or the body stops
being binary. So the constraint lives in the handler and is documented as a
response, and a generator reading this will believe an empty body is valid.

ShareResponse.description: A share as the API describes it. Never carries the content.

code.description: The retrieval code, as a person reads it.

expires_at.description: When it stops being served, RFC 3339, or `null` to live until deleted.

has_password.description: Whether a password must be presented to retrieve it.

management_token.description:
Token that lets an anonymous uploader delete this share.

**Shown once, at creation, and only when nobody was signed in.** Only its
digest is stored. Without it a mistaken anonymous upload could never be
taken back.

path.description:
Where the share lives, relative to this instance's origin.

Relative on purpose: the server does not know what host it is reached
through, and guessing wrong behind a reverse proxy produces links that
do not work. Whoever calls this already knows the origin they called.

size_bytes.description: Size of the content in bytes.

use_count.description: How many times it has been retrieved.

uses_remaining.description: How many retrievals remain, or `null` for unlimited.

StatsResponse.description:
What one instance is holding, at a glance.

# Why this is not a metrics endpoint

Four numbers an operator can act on, not a time series. "Am I near the
quota", "how many people are on here", "is the sweep keeping up" — the
questions somebody asks before deciding whether to change a setting. Anything
that wants graphs wants Prometheus, and that is a different endpoint with a
different shape.

administrators.description: How many of those administer the instance.

live_invites.description: How many invites could still admit somebody.

live_shares.description:
How many a visitor could still open.

The gap between this and `shares` is what the sweep has not reached yet,
which is worth seeing: a large one means retention is longer than
somebody expected, or the sweep is not running.

quota_bytes.description:
The ceiling from `storage.max_total_bytes`, or `null` when unset.

`null` is not "unlimited" so much as "nobody said" — and on an instance
that takes anonymous uploads, that is the combination the start-up
warning is about.

shares.description: How many shares exist, including ones nobody can open any more.

stored_bytes.description: Bytes of uploaded content still on the store.

expires_at.description: When the authorisation stops being honoured, RFC 3339.

ticket.description: Present it as `X-Share-Ticket`, or as `?t=` on a download link.

uses_remaining.description: How many retrievals remain after this one.

TokenResponse.description: An issued token, as a listing describes it. Never carries the secret.

display_prefix.description:
Leading characters of the secret, so a person can tell two tokens apart
without the service having to store either of them.

expires_at.description: When it stops being accepted, or `null` to live until revoked.

last_used_at.description: When it was last accepted, if ever.

revoked_at.description: When it was revoked, if it was.

is_admin.description: Whether this account administers the instance.

bearer.description: An API token from `POST /api/v1/tokens`, sent as `Authorization: Bearer tsk_…`. Shown once at creation.

session.description: Set by `POST /auth/login`. A browser sends it automatically; it is `HttpOnly`, so page scripts cannot read or set it.
session.name: tessera_session

info.description: Anonymous file courier. Upload a file or a note, hand out a retrieval code, and the payload destroys itself once it expires or runs out of retrievals.
info.title: Tessera API

# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when the caller is not an
administrator or used a bearer token, `404` when this instance has no
administration.

403.description: Not an administrator, or authenticated with an API token

post.description:
# Why this exists when the CLI already does it

The command line is the rescue path — it works with the service stopped and
needs nothing but the database file. This is the ordinary path: somebody
letting a friend in should not have to reach a shell on the box.

# Errors

`400` when `uses` is below one or the lifetime is beyond a calendar, `401`
when nothing was signed in, `403` when the caller is not an administrator or
used a bearer token, `404` when this instance has no administration.

403.description: Not an administrator, or authenticated with an API token

post.summary: Mints an invite code and returns it, once.

delete.description:
The accounts it already admitted stay: an account created through a code does
not depend on the code still existing. What this stops is the code letting
anybody else in, which is what somebody who posted one in the wrong chat
window wants.

# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when the caller is not an
administrator or used a bearer token, `404` when no invite has that
identifier.

403.description: Not an administrator, or authenticated with an API token

get.description:
# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when the caller is not an
administrator or used a bearer token, `404` when this instance has no
administration.

403.description: Not an administrator, or authenticated with an API token

get.summary: Reports what this instance is holding.

get.description:
# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when the caller is not an
administrator or used a bearer token, `404` when this instance has no
administration.

403.description: Not an administrator, or authenticated with an API token

delete.description:
# What goes with it and what does not

Sessions and API tokens are deleted by the database. Shares are not: their
owner column is `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so what somebody uploaded becomes an
anonymous share and keeps working for whoever holds the code. Deleting an
account is about the account, and taking somebody's files off the internet in
the same motion would be a second decision made silently.

# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when the caller is not an
administrator or used a bearer token, `404` when no account has that
identifier, `409` when this would leave the instance with no administrator.

403.description: Not an administrator, or authenticated with an API token

409.description: That would leave the instance with no administrator

patch.description:
# Why the last one cannot be removed

An instance with no administrator cannot be repaired through the API — there
is no endpoint left that would let anybody grant the flag back. The way out
is the command line against the database file, which an operator who locked
themselves out of a container may not have. So the case is refused rather
than allowed and regretted.

Removing your own flag while somebody else still has it is allowed: that is
a person stepping down, not an accident.

# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when the caller is not an
administrator or used a bearer token, `404` when no account has that
identifier, `409` when this would leave the instance with none.

200.description: The account as it now stands

403.description: Not an administrator, or authenticated with an API token

409.description: That would leave the instance with no administrator

patch.summary: Grants or removes the administrator flag.

post.description:
# Errors

`401` when the credentials do not match, `429` when too many attempts have
failed, `404` when the instance has no accounts.

400.description: The body is not the shape this expects

post.description:
# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in.

patch.description:
Every other session is ended, and a fresh one is issued so the caller stays
signed in where they are. Whoever knew the old password may be holding a
session, and changing a password is how a person says they want that to stop.

# Errors

`401` when the current password is wrong, `403` when authenticated with an
API token, `400` when the new password fails the policy.

400.description: The new password fails the policy

403.description: Not permitted with an API token

post.description:
# Why this always answers the same way

`202` whether or not the address belongs to an account, and whether or not
the mail could be handed to the relay. Any other shape turns this endpoint
into a way of asking "does this person have an account here" — which for a
file courier is a question about who uses it, answerable by anyone, at any
rate the throttle allows.

The cost is that a typo produces no feedback. That is the right way round:
somebody who mistyped their own address will notice when no mail arrives,
and nobody learns anything from the response either way.

# Errors

`404` when this instance sends no mail — the route is not mounted at all, so
this is the router's answer rather than the handler's. `429` when this
address has already been sent as many links as the window allows.

202.description: Accepted; a link is sent if that address has an account

400.description: The body is not the shape this expects

429.description: Too many links have been sent to this address

post.summary: Sends a password reset link, if there is an account and mail is configured.

post.description:
Every session belonging to the account is ended. Somebody asking to reset a
password is usually saying they have lost control of it, and leaving the
sessions alone would leave whoever had it signed in.

# Errors

`400` when the token is unknown, spent or expired, or the new password fails
the policy. `404` when this instance sends no mail.

400.description: The link is not usable, or the password fails the policy

post.summary: Sets a new password from a reset link.

post.description:
# Errors

`404` when the instance has no accounts, `403` when registration is closed,
`409` when the name or address is taken, `400` when a value fails its rule.

201.description: Account created and signed in; only where this instance sends no mail

202.description: Accepted; a confirmation link is sent if that address is free

429.description: Too many messages have been sent to this address

post.summary: Creates an account and signs it in.

post.description:
# Why the checks happen here and not when the link was sent

Nothing was reserved while the message sat in an inbox. Reserving the name
would have made "register and never confirm" a free way to lock every good
name away, with nothing an operator could do about it. The price is this:
the name is checked against today's accounts, and somebody can be told at
this point that it went to another person. That is rare, it is recoverable,
and it is a much smaller problem than the alternative.

# Errors

`400` when the link is unknown, spent or expired, `403` when registration was
closed while this was waiting, `409` when the name went to somebody else in
the meantime, `404` when this instance sends no mail.

400.description: The link is not usable, or the body is not the shape this expects

403.description: Registration was closed while this link was waiting

409.description: The name was taken while this was waiting

post.summary: Turns a confirmed registration into an account.

get.description:
# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in.

Answers to everyone, signed in or not — a client needs this before it can
know whether logging in is even possible. An administrator gets one extra
field; see [`Capabilities::storage_remaining_bytes`].

# Errors

Only when the storage total cannot be read, which is an administrator's
request against a database that is not answering.
get.summary: Reports which optional parts of the service this instance exposes.

delete.description:
The button somebody presses when they think another person is signed in as
them. It spares the browser doing the asking, because being logged out by
your own attempt to log everybody else out is a poor way to find out it
worked.

# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when a bearer token was used.

403.description: Authenticated with an API token, or a password change is due

delete.summary: Ends every session except the one asking.

get.description:
# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when a bearer token was used or the
account still owes a password change.

403.description: Authenticated with an API token, or a password change is due

get.summary: Lists the caller's sign-ins, newest first.

delete.description:
# Why an identifier that is not yours is a `404`

The same answer as one that never existed, and as one that is not an
identifier at all. Telling them apart would make this endpoint a way to ask
which identifiers exist and who they belong to.

# Why a session that had already finished is a `204`

The caller asked for it to stop working, and it does not work. Answering
`404` for a row they can see in their own list would be a puzzle, and would
mean a list that went stale between loading and clicking reports a problem
where there is none. Nothing is written, so the time it ended does not move.

# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when a bearer token was used, `404`
when no session of the caller's has that identifier.

403.description: Authenticated with an API token, or a password change is due

404.description: No session of yours has that id

delete.summary: Ends one of the caller's sessions.

get.description:
# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in.
get.summary: Lists the caller's shares, newest first.

post.description:
# Errors

`401` when the instance requires an account to upload, `400` when a parameter
is unusable, `413` when the body exceeds the configured limit, `409` when no
unused code could be found.

parameters.description:
Original file name. Its presence is what makes this a file share rather
than a note.
parameters.name: filename

parameters.description: Display name, shown on the share page and in the link preview.
parameters.name: title

parameters.name: language

parameters.name: expires_in_hours

parameters.description:
How many times it may be retrieved. Omit for unlimited; `1` is
burn-after-reading.
parameters.name: max_uses

requestBody.description: The content itself. Send the file as the raw body — no wrapper, no encoding.

401.description: This instance requires an account to upload

507.description: This instance is out of room

delete.description:
Accepts either the owning account or, for an anonymous share, the management
token from creation — sent as `X-Share-Management-Token`.

# Errors

`404` when no share of the caller's has that code. Deliberately the same
answer as "somebody else's": distinguishing them would confirm which codes
exist.

404.description: No share of yours has that code

delete.summary: Deletes a share, and whatever it put in the blob store.

get.description:
This is what the share page reads to decide what to render. It never
consumes, so a link preview, a prefetch or a mail-scanner following the URL
cannot destroy a one-time share.

# Errors

`404` when nothing has that code, `410` when it has expired or run out,
`401` when it is password-protected and the password given was wrong.

parameters.description: The share's password, if it has one
parameters.name: X-Share-Password

429.description: Too many lookups or password attempts

post.description:
# Why this is a separate step

One authorisation costs one retrieval; the ticket it returns is then good for
every request the transfer needs — each `Range`, each resumption, each retry.
Counting requests instead would let a resumed download spend three uses of a
share that allows three.

# Errors

`401` when the password is wrong, `404` when nothing has that code, `410`
when it has expired or run out.

parameters.description: The share's password, if it has one
parameters.name: X-Share-Password

429.description: Too many lookups or password attempts

post.summary: Spends one retrieval and returns a ticket for the transfer.

`401` when nothing was signed in — which is also what an instance with
accounts turned off answers, since there is nobody to be. `403` when the
account still owes a password change.
get.summary: Lists the caller's tokens, newest first.

# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when authenticated with a token
rather than a session, `400` when the name or lifetime is unusable.

201.description: Issued; the secret is shown only here

400.description: The name or lifetime is unusable

403.description: Authenticated with an API token, or a password change is due

# Errors

`401` when nothing was signed in, `403` when authenticated with a token,
`404` when no live token of the caller's has that id.

403.description: Authenticated with an API token, or a password change is due

404.description: No live token of yours has that id

get.description:
Deliberately both a liveness and a readiness probe: the process only reaches
[`ServiceStatus::Ready`] once migrations have run, and it flips to
[`ServiceStatus::Draining`] the moment a shutdown signal arrives, so an
orchestrator can stop routing before the listener actually closes.

# Errors

Returns [`Error::Unavailable`] (503) while starting up or draining, and when
the database round-trip fails.

503.description: Starting up, draining, or a dependency is unreachable

get.summary: Reports whether the service is ready to take traffic.
